A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Doctor-R1 research, with matching core methods and benchmark results. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, component ablations, scaling experiments and a human preference study in Section 4 and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds physician assessments, further ablations, evaluator comparisons, failure analyses and computational measurements.

M1.justification: The multi-agent environment, GRPO training, two-tier reward architecture and experience retrieval/storage procedure remain unchanged. The Llama experiment applies the existing framework to another backbone; additional component tests and explanations do not introduce a revised proposed method.

E1.justification: The training and evaluation coverage remains KaMed-derived dialogue data, HealthBench Main/Hard, MAQuE, MedQA and medical MMLU questions. Physician judging, additional backbone experiments and examples from existing trajectories change evaluation or analysis, without establishing new clinical datasets, populations or task environments.

E2.justification: GPT-5 replaces GPT-o3 in the HealthBench Main, HealthBench Hard and MAQuE comparisons. v2 also adds evaluated SFT and PPO baselines and retrieval/reward variants, substantially expanding the comparisons used to isolate component contributions. Figure 3 no longer reports DeepSeek-V3 in the pairwise human comparison.

E3.justification: v2 introduces physician scoring of 80 sampled trajectories, categorical retrieval-utility assessment, and a 40-case cross-evaluator study (Appendix E). Additional protocols include Llama-3.1-8B experiments, safety-violation and empathy measurements, and a 200-case inference-cost evaluation. The existing benchmark sampling and deterministic decoding settings are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's component-removal, similarity-retrieval and scaling studies, v2 tests SFT/PPO versus GRPO, state-only versus random/full retrieval, backbone transferability, and removal of safety vetoes or soft-skill rewards. It also adds evaluator validation, retrieval examples, concrete failure and simulation-fidelity analyses, and computational-overhead studies (Appendices D–I).

E5.justification: Appendix E.3 newly reports Spearman rank correlations between the Qwen3-8B evaluator and GPT-4.1/human judgments. This adds statistical agreement assessment beyond v1's win-rate aggregation. Neither version reports repeated-training-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: Doctor-R1's headline scores remain 36.29 on HealthBench Main, 18.73 on Hard and 60.00 accuracy on MAQuE. v2 adds GPT-5 results of 46.38, 29.57 and 67.00 respectively, plus optimization, transfer, physician, safety, retrieval-utility and runtime results. An existing result also changes: similarity-only retrieval's Health Data Tasks score is 26.96 in v1 Table 6 and 24.96 in v2 Table 8.

T1.justification: The POMDP formulation and numbered equations remain unchanged. Appendix D.1 adds a qualitative explanation of GRPO's purported advantages over SFT and PPO, but supplies no new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list replace the claim of human-preferred dialogue with a claim of expert-validated clinical capability and patient-centric performance. The central contributions—unified inquiry and decision-making, experiential RL, and parameter-efficient benchmark performance—remain intact.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning action-bearing retrieval, irrelevant-experience interference, GRPO optimization and backbone transferability. It documents specific omission and hallucination failures, observed reward-hacking behavior, and a computational cost-benefit argument. These considerably extend v1's component explanations and general limitations.

D1.justification: v2 adds an explicit code/model release statement and model-weight link, training/inference timing details, and disclosure of approximately 50 manually reviewed high-reward trajectories per day. Most hardware, prompts and hyperparameters remain unchanged; the previously stated reward-model/critic learning rate is removed, without establishing that the underlying training changed.

R1.justification: Section 6 adds a feature comparison matrix and distinguishes single-turn RL, test-time adaptation and interactive agents, incorporating FineMedLM-o1, Med-PRM and MedAdapter. It revises the positioning against DoctorAgent-RL: v1 characterizes it as focused on static answering, whereas v2 acknowledges interaction and emphasizes differential diagnosis and experiential learning as distinguishing capabilities.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, human-evaluation discussion and related work receive localized revisions. Appendices gain dedicated ablation and human-evaluation subsections, alongside LLM-usage and reproducibility statements. The main section sequence and most existing method prose remain stable; much of the expansion is new scientific content.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is revised, and Figure 3 becomes a combined patient-preference and physician-rating display. v2 expands the retrieval table's columns and adds optimization, transfer, reward, evaluator and overhead tables plus boxed case studies. Existing scaling plots and the original clinical case table are retained, with relocation or renumbering.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence missing from v1: physician assessment supplements lay preferences, while optimization, retrieval and reward controls directly test central component claims. Concrete failure examples and cost measurements also make limitations and practical tradeoffs clearer. Some new summaries overstate the evidence: Appendix E.3 claims Doctor-R1 ranks first among open models under every judge, although Tables 14–15 give Baichuan-M2 a higher human mean, 4.31 versus 4.30. This reporting weakness limits the conclusions but does not outweigh the substantial gains in validation.
